title: FIFOs
summary: The FIFO is the most common memory structure in digital design: a queue built from a dual-port memory and two pointers. This topic shows the ring buffer step by step, how full and empty are detected, how a FIFO looks in waveforms, why asynchronous FIFOs need Gray-code pointers — and a complete synchronous FIFO in SystemVerilog.
objectives: Explain a FIFO as a ring buffer with write and read pointers.
Detect full and empty with a wrap bit.
Explain why asynchronous FIFOs use Gray-code pointers and synchronisers.
Write a synchronous FIFO in SystemVerilog.

blocks.md: A **FIFO** (first in, first out) is a queue: words leave in the order they arrived. FIFOs connect blocks that produce and consume data at **different moments or rates** — a network port and a processor, a camera and a frame buffer, two clock domains. Inside, a FIFO is a dual-port memory plus two counters.

rows: between a fast producer and a slow consumer
in front of a bus or memory controller
queues requests while the slave is busy
blocks.caption: Where FIFOs are used

subsections.title: A ring buffer with two pointers

blocks.md: A FIFO stores its words in a memory that is used as a **ring**: a **write pointer** shows where the next word goes, a **read pointer** where the oldest word is. Both only count up and wrap around.

steps.title: Reset
steps.md: Both pointers point to slot 0: the FIFO is empty.

steps.title: Push
steps.md: Three words are written; the write pointer moves on.

steps.title: Pop
steps.md: The oldest word A leaves; the read pointer moves on.

steps.title: Wrap around
steps.md: After slot 7 the write pointer continues at slot 0 — its extra **wrap bit** flips to 1.

steps.title: Full
steps.md: The write pointer reaches the read pointer's slot with a different wrap bit: all 8 slots are used.

steps.title: Empty again
steps.md: After 8 pops the pointers are equal again: empty.

blocks.md:
If pointers only counted slots 0–7, *equal pointers* could mean both **empty** and **full**. The trick is one **extra bit**:

> empty = (wptr == rptr)  ·  full = same slot bits, different wrap bit

items.title: Almost-full and almost-empty
items.md: Many FIFOs add flags that warn a few words **before** full or empty — so a pipelined producer can stop in time. They compare the pointer difference with a threshold.

items.title: Standard and first-word-fall-through
items.md: A **standard** FIFO delivers the word one clock after the pop request. A **first-word-fall-through (FWFT)** FIFO already shows the oldest word on its output; the pop only removes it.

items.title: Overflow and underflow
items.md: A push into a full FIFO or a pop from an empty one must be **ignored** (and often flagged as an error). The design below simply ignores them.

blocks.caption: Three pushes, then three pops; dout follows one clock after each pop

blocks.title: Simultaneous push and pop
blocks.md: A push and a pop in the same clock are allowed (when not full / not empty): the number of words stays the same, both pointers move.

blocks.caption: Each domain owns its pointer; the other side sees a synchronised Gray-coded copy

blocks.md:
When writer and reader have **different clocks**, each pointer must be passed to the other domain to compute full and empty. A binary counter changing from 0111 to 1000 flips four bits at once — sampled at the wrong moment it can be read as any value. **Gray code** changes only one bit per step, so after a two-flip-flop **synchroniser** the other side sees either the old or the new value — never a wrong one. Full and empty are then slightly **pessimistic** but always safe.

The full design is covered in *Designing with Memories* (training 4).

blocks.md: A complete synchronous FIFO: storage in a memory array (a simple dual-port RAM), two pointers with a wrap bit, and the flags:

items.title: Where is the memory?
items.md: `mem` with one write (`do_wr`) and one registered read (`do_rd`) per clock — exactly the simple dual-port RAM of Topic 6, so synthesis can use block RAM or an SRAM macro.

items.title: Why `wptr[AW-1:0]` as address?
items.md: The lower bits are the slot; the top bit is only the wrap flag for full/empty.

items.title: How would you add a word counter?
items.md: count = wptr − rptr (with AW+1 bits). It gives almost-full / almost-empty flags by comparison.
